claim: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a plant hormone that regulates plant growth and development and mediates abiotic stress responses.
source: Abscisic acid (ABA) is a plant hormone that regulates plant growth and development and mediates abiotic stress responses.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in plant biology supported by extensive literature, as indicated by the references throughout the manuscript.

claim: ABAleons are ABA-specific optogenetic reporters that instantaneously convert the phytohormone-triggered interaction of ABA receptors with PP2C-type phosphatases to send a fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) signal in response to ABA.
source: We have developed ABAleons: ABA-specific optogenetic reporters that instantaneously convert the phytohormone-triggered interaction of ABA receptors with PP2C-type phosphatases to send a fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) signal in response to ABA.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the design and experimental validation presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ABAleons have ABA affinities in the range of 100–600 nM.
source: We report the design, engineering and use of ABAleons with ABA affinities in the range of 100–600 nM to map ABA concentration changes in plant tissues with spatial and temporal resolution.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro characterization data showing K′d values for different ABAleon variants.

claim: High ABAleon expression can partially repress Arabidopsis ABA responses.
source: High ABAleon expression can partially repress Arabidopsis ABA responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ABA sensitivity analyses showing that ABAleon2.1 plants exhibit reduced ABA sensitivity in seed germination and seedling growth assays, with the degree of hyposensitivity correlating with expression levels.

claim: ABAleons report ABA concentration differences in distinct cell types.
source: ABAleons report ABA concentration differences in distinct cell types, ABA concentration increases in response to low humidity and NaCl in guard cells and to NaCl and osmotic stress in roots and ABA transport from the hypocotyl to the shoot and root.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing different emission ratios in various tissues and cell types.

claim: ABAleons report ABA concentration increases in response to low humidity and NaCl in guard cells.
source: ABAleons report ABA concentration differences in distinct cell types, ABA concentration increases in response to low humidity and NaCl in guard cells and to NaCl and osmotic stress in roots and ABA transport from the hypocotyl to the shoot and root.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing ABAleon2.1 emission ratio changes in guard cells after humidity drop and NaCl treatment.

claim: ABAleons report ABA concentration increases in response to NaCl and osmotic stress in roots.
source: ABAleons report ABA concentration differences in distinct cell types, ABA concentration increases in response to low humidity and NaCl in guard cells and to NaCl and osmotic stress in roots and ABA transport from the hypocotyl to the shoot and root.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing ABAleon2.1 emission ratio changes in root tissues after NaCl and sorbitol treatments.

claim: ABAleons report ABA transport from the hypocotyl to the shoot and root.
source: ABAleons report ABA concentration differences in distinct cell types, ABA concentration increases in response to low humidity and NaCl in guard cells and to NaCl and osmotic stress in roots and ABA transport from the hypocotyl to the shoot and root.
evidence: This is demonstrated by long-distance ABA transport experiments showing directional ABA movement.

claim: Auxin is best characterized among plant hormones in terms of its distribution and transport.
source: Among plant hormones, auxin is best characterized in terms of its distribution and transport (Vanneste and Friml, 2009), analyzed using reporter constructs for auxin-induced gene expression or protein degradation (Ulmasov et al., 1997; Brunoud et al., 2012; Wend et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature on auxin research.

claim: Reporter genes for ABA-induced gene expression (pRD29A/B, pRAB18 and pAtHB6) are used to study ABA responses.
source: Reporter genes developed for ABA-induced gene expression (pRD29A/B, pRAB18 and pAtHB6) are also used (Lång and Palva, 1992; Yamaguchi-Shinozaki and Shinozaki, 1993; Ishitani et al., 1997; Christmann et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2011; Duan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies using these reporters.

claim: Promoter-linked reporters respond indirectly and slowly to their respective plant hormone.
source: Despite their potential, such promoter-linked reporters respond indirectly and slowly to their respective plant hormone.
evidence: This is a known limitation of transcriptional reporters based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: No reporters for direct visualization of any plant hormone have yet been developed prior to this study.
source: However, no reporters for direct visualization of any plant hormone have yet been developed.
evidence: This statement establishes the novelty of the work and is based on the authors' knowledge of the field at the time of publication.

claim: During land colonization, plants adopted ABA as a hormone to signal stress due to limited water supply.
source: During land colonization, plants adopted ABA as a hormone to signal stress due to limited water supply (Cutler et al., 2010; Raghavendra et al., 2010; Hauser et al., 2011).
evidence: This evolutionary perspective is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ABA is integrated into a complex signaling network that transcriptionally and post-translationally regulates seed germination, root development and stomatal aperture.
source: ABA is integrated into a complex signaling network that transcriptionally and post-translationally regulates seed germination, root development and stomatal aperture (Hetherington and Woodward, 2003; Cutler et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2010; Raghavendra et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature on ABA signaling.

claim: In Arabidopsis, ABA is synthesized primarily in vascular tissues of roots and leaves, in guard cells and in seeds.
source: In Arabidopsis, ABA is synthesized primarily in vascular tissues of roots and leaves, in guard cells and in seeds (Sauter et al., 2001; Endo et al., 2008; Seo and Koshiba, 2011; Bauer et al., 2013; Boursiac et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies on ABA biosynthesis.

claim: ABA catabolism includes hydroxylation pathways and glucose conjugation leading to less- or inactive compounds.
source: ABA catabolism includes hydroxylation pathways and glucose conjugation leading to less- or inactive compounds (Nambara and Marion-Poll, 2005; Kepka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on ABA metabolism.

claim: ABA-glucose ester is stored in the vacuole and was reported to be rapidly hydrolyzed by β-glucosidases.
source: ABA-glucose ester is stored in the vacuole and was reported to be rapidly hydrolyzed by β-glucosidases (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Direct measurements of rapid ABA release are missing.
source: However, direct measurements of rapid ABA release are missing.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the field that the current study addresses.

claim: ABA transporters contribute to ABA export from the vasculature and import into guard cells.
source: Recently identified ABA transporters contribute to ABA export from the vasculature and import into guard cells (Kang et al., 2010; Kuromori et al., 2010, 2011; Kanno et al., 2012; Boursiac et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies on ABA transporters.

claim: In response to water limitations ABA concentrations increase.
source: In response to water limitations ABA concentrations increase (Harris et al., 1988; Harris and Outlaw, 1991; Christmann et al., 2007; Forcat et al., 2008; Ikegami et al., 2009; Geng et al., 2013) and decrease upon stress relief (Harris and Outlaw, 1991; Endo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies measuring ABA levels under stress.

claim: ABA concentrations decrease upon stress relief.
source: In response to water limitations ABA concentrations increase (Harris et al., 1988; Harris and Outlaw, 1991; Christmann et al., 2007; Forcat et al., 2008; Ikegami et al., 2009; Geng et al., 2013) and decrease upon stress relief (Harris and Outlaw, 1991; Endo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Direct evidence for conditionally triggered changes in local ABA concentrations and time-resolved data for ABA re-distribution in vivo are lacking.
source: Despite recent progress on ABA synthesis and transport, direct evidence for conditionally triggered changes in local ABA concentrations and time-resolved data for ABA re-distribution in vivo are lacking.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the field that the current study addresses.

claim: ABA is perceived by members of a protein family designated as PYRABACTIN RESISTANCE 1 (PYR1)/PYR1-LIKE (PYL)/REGULATORY COMPONENT OF ABA RECEPTOR (RCAR).
source: ABA is perceived by members of a protein family designated as PYRABACTIN RESISTANCE 1 (PYR1)/PYR1-LIKE (PYL)/REGULATORY COMPONENT OF ABA RECEPTOR (RCAR), which in the presence of ABA negatively regulate Clade A TYPE 2C PROTEIN PHOSPHATASES (PP2Cs) (Ma et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on ABA receptors.

claim: PYR/PYL/RCARs in the presence of ABA negatively regulate Clade A TYPE 2C PROTEIN PHOSPHATASES (PP2Cs).
source: ABA is perceived by members of a protein family designated as PYRABACTIN RESISTANCE 1 (PYR1)/PYR1-LIKE (PYL)/REGULATORY COMPONENT OF ABA RECEPTOR (RCAR), which in the presence of ABA negatively regulate Clade A TYPE 2C PROTEIN PHOSPHATASES (PP2Cs) (Ma et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on ABA signaling.

claim: Inhibition of PP2Cs enables the activation of SNF1-RELATED KINASES 2 (SnRK2s).
source: Inhibition of PP2Cs enables the activation of SNF1-RELATED KINASES 2 (SnRK2s) (Fujii et al., 2009; Umezawa et al., 2009; Vlad et al., 2009), that target transcription factors, ion channels and NADPH oxidases (Kobayashi et al., 2005; Furihata et al., 2006; Geiger et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Sato et al., 2009; Sirichandra et al., 2009, 2010; Brandt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies on ABA signaling.

claim: SnRK2s target transcription factors, ion channels and NADPH oxidases.
source: Inhibition of PP2Cs enables the activation of SNF1-RELATED KINASES 2 (SnRK2s) (Fujii et al., 2009; Umezawa et al., 2009; Vlad et al., 2009), that target transcription factors, ion channels and NADPH oxidases (Kobayashi et al., 2005; Furihata et al., 2006; Geiger et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Sato et al., 2009; Sirichandra et al., 2009, 2010; Brandt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: PYR/PYL/RCARs contain an internal ligand-binding pocket flanked by two conserved loops, the 'Pro-cap/gate' and the 'Leu-lock/latch'.
source: PYR/PYL/RCARs contain an internal ligand-binding pocket flanked by two conserved loops, the 'Pro-cap/gate' and the 'Leu-lock/latch' (Melcher et al., 2009; Nishimura et al., 2009; Santiago et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of ABA receptors.

claim: ABA binding triggers loops to rearrange, closing the lid over ABA.
source: ABA binding triggers these loops to rearrange, closing the lid over ABA.
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The conformational change and rearranged protein surface favors PP2C binding over receptor dimerization.
source: The conformational change and rearranged protein surface favors PP2C binding over receptor dimerization (Melcher et al., 2009; Nishimura et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: In the ABA receptor–phosphatase complex, a conserved Trp residue from the PP2C inserts between the 'Pro-cap/gate' and the 'Leu-lock/latch' to further enclose the ABA.
source: In the resultant ABA receptor–phosphatase complex, a conserved Trp residue from the PP2C inserts between the 'Pro-cap/gate' and the 'Leu-lock/latch' to further enclose the ABA (Melcher et al., 2009; Miyazono et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: ABAleon1.1 has a dynamic range of approximately 15% and an apparent ABA affinity K′d of approximately 300 nM.
source: For ABAleon1.1 a dynamic range of ∼ 15 % was recorded with an apparent ABA affinity K′d of ∼ 300 nM (Figure 1C,E,F).
evidence: This is directly measured from in vitro characterization experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: ABAleon2.1 exhibited a dynamic range of approximately 9% and a K′d of approximately 100 nM.
source: ABAleon2.1 exhibited a dynamic range of ∼ 9 % and a K′d of ∼ 100 nM (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is directly measured from in vitro characterization experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Application of ABA rapidly and clearly induced emission ratio changes of approximately 8% when analyzing ABAleon2.1 at 1 µM ABA.
source: In plate reader-based analyses, application of ABA rapidly and clearly induced emission ratio changes of ∼ 8 % when analyzing ABAleon2.1 at 1 µM ABA (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is directly measured from kinetic experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ABAleon1.1 exhibited phosphatase activity comparable to PYR1 and ΔNABI1 when combined in a 1:1 molar ratio.
source: ABAleon1.1 exhibited phosphatase activity comparable to PYR1 and ΔNABI1 when combined in a 1:1 molar ratio (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is directly measured from phosphatase activity assays shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In the presence of 5 µM ABA phosphatase activity of ABAleon1.1 was inhibited to 50% of initial activity.
source: In the presence of 5 µM ABA phosphatase activity was inhibited to 50 % of initial activity (Figure 1H; Ma et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009; Santiago et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is directly measured from phosphatase activity assays shown in Figure 1H and is consistent with published studies.

claim: The ABI1D413L mutation in ABAleon2.1 enabled the design of an ABA-reporter without detectable phosphatase activity.
source: However, the predicted phosphatase inactive ABI1D413L mutation in ABAleon2.1 enabled the design of an ABA-reporter without detectable phosphatase activity (Figure 1H), which was considered to be preferable for use in plants.
evidence: This is directly measured from phosphatase activity assays shown in Figure 1H.

claim: 15 min after a drop in humidity ABAleon2.1 emission ratios decreased approximately 3% in guard cells.
source: 15 min after a drop in humidity ABAleon2.1 emission ratios decreased ∼ 3 % in guard cells and did not change when analyzed at the 30 min time point (Figure 9A,B), indicating fast ABA concentration adjustments in response to humidity changes.
evidence: This is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: In 4 h stress treatments of detached leaves 100 mM NaCl and 10 µM ABA induced a 5–6% ABAleon2.1 emission ratio change in guard cells.
source: In 4 h stress treatments of detached leaves 100 mM NaCl and 10 µM ABA induced a 5–6 % ABAleon2.1 emission ratio change in guard cells (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: This is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 9C,D.

claim: 300 mM sorbitol did not induce any detectable changes in ABAleon2.1 emission ratios in guard cells.
source: In contrast, 300 mM sorbitol did not induce any detectable changes (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: This is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 9C,D.

claim: 100 mM NaCl or 300 mM sorbitol induced ABAleon2.1 emission ratio changes of 3–6% in the root maturation zone.
source: In these analyses 100 mM NaCl or 300 mM sorbitol induced ABAleon2.1 emission ratio changes of 3–6 % in the root maturation zone compared to 7 % changes in response to 10 µM ABA (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 9F.

claim: In the root elongation zone, responses to 100 mM NaCl and 300 mM sorbitol were 7–8% while 10 µM ABA induced ABAleon2.1 emission ratio changes of 5–6%.
source: In the root elongation zone, responses to 100 mM NaCl and 300 mM sorbitol were 7–8 % while 10 µM ABA induced ABAleon2.1 emission ratio changes of 5–6 % (Figure 9H).
evidence: This is directly measured from experiments shown in Figure 9H.

claim: The speed of ABA transport within the hypocotyl was approximately 16 µm/min.
source: From three independent experiments the rate of ABA transport in the hypocotyl was calculated as 16.4 ± 0.8 µm/min.
evidence: This is calculated from time-resolved ABAleon2.1 response data in the hypocotyl.

claim: ABA transport from the root maturation zone to the shoot could not be detected within three hours under the imposed conditions.
source: Furthermore, ABA transport from the root maturation zone to the shoot could not be detected within three hours (Figure 6D,I,J).
evidence: This is directly observed from long-distance transport experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: ABAleon2.1 plants exhibited a reduced sensitivity to exogenously applied ABA in seed germination, cotyledon expansion and growth assays, but not in stomatal closure assays.
source: Transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing ABAleon2.1 exhibited a reduced sensitivity to exogenously applied ABA in seed germination, cotyledon expansion and growth assays, but not in stomatal closure assays (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ABA sensitivity assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: The degree of reduced ABA sensitivity correlated with increasing ABAleon2.1 expression levels in two independent transgenic lines.
source: The degree of reduced ABA sensitivity correlated with increasing ABAleon2.1 expression levels in two independent transgenic lines (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing ABA sensitivity and expression levels in different lines shown in Figure 5.

claim: ABA-induced ABAleon2.1 ratio changes in the root maturation zone were accelerated in the pyr1-1/pyl1-1/pyl2-1/pyl4-1 mutant.
source: Surprisingly, ABA-induced ABAleon2.1 ratio changes in the root maturation zone were accelerated in the pyr1-1/pyl1-1/pyl2-1/pyl4-1 mutant (Figure 4).
evidence: This is directly measured from experiments comparing Col-0 and pyl4ple mutant shown in Figure 4.

claim: Half saturation of ABAleon2.1 was reached 16 min after ABA application in Col-0, while this appeared within 7 min in the pyl4ple mutant.
source: Half saturation of ABAleon2.1 was reached 16 min after ABA application in Col-0, while this appeared within 7 min in the pyl4ple mutant (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is calculated from fitted response curves shown in Figure 4.

claim: ABAleon2.13 harboring the PYR1V83H mutation exhibited a reduced ABA affinity (K′d approximately 3–4 µM).
source: Of the seven analyzed ABAleon2.1 mutants, PYR1V83H in ABAleon2.13 and PYR1H115A in ABAleon2.15 were of particular interest, as these mutants exhibited a reduced ABA affinity (K′d ∼ 3–4 µM of ABAleon2.13 and ∼ 500–600 nM of ABAleon2.15; Figure 7E; Table 1).
evidence: This is directly measured from in vitro characterization experiments shown in Figure 7E and Table 1.

claim: ABAleon2.15 harboring the PYR1H115A mutation exhibited a reduced ABA affinity (K′d approximately 500–600 nM).
source: Of the seven analyzed ABAleon2.1 mutants, PYR1V83H in ABAleon2.13 and PYR1H115A in ABAleon2.15 were of particular interest, as these mutants exhibited a reduced ABA affinity (K′d ∼ 3–4 µM of ABAleon2.13 and ∼ 500–600 nM of ABAleon2.15; Figure 7E; Table 1).
evidence: This is directly measured from in vitro characterization experiments shown in Figure 7E and Table 1.

claim: ABAleon2.15 exhibited an apparent affinity for (−)-ABA of approximately 30 µM, which was 50-fold reduced compared to the (+)-ABA affinity.
source: Remarkably, ABAleon2.15 harboring the PYR1H115A mutation exhibited an apparent affinity for (−)-ABA of ∼ 30 µM (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1F,G), which was 50-fold reduced compared to the (+)-ABA affinity (K′d ∼ 0.6 µ M) (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D) suggesting, that PYR1H115 has an important function in ABA stereospecificity.
evidence: This is directly measured from in vitro characterization experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: PYR1H115 has an important function in ABA stereospecificity.
source: Remarkably, ABAleon2.15 harboring the PYR1H115A mutation exhibited an apparent affinity for (−)-ABA of ∼ 30 µM (Figure 7G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1F,G), which was 50-fold reduced compared to the (+)-ABA affinity (K′d ∼ 0.6 µ M) (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D) suggesting, that PYR1H115 has an important function in ABA stereospecificity.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential binding of (+)- and (−)-ABA by ABAleon2.15 with the PYR1H115A mutation.

claim: ABAleon2.15 is the best candidate for a low affinity (K′d approximately 600 nM) ABA-reporter.
source: Thus, ABAleon2.15 is the best candidate for a low affinity (K′d ∼ 600 nM) ABA-reporter.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the performance of different ABAleon variants in planta.

claim: Application of ABA had no impact on ABAleon2.1 absorbance.
source: In vitro application of ABA had no impact on ABAleon2.1 absorbance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly measured from absorbance spectra shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ABA-induced ABAleon1.1 emission ratio changes were stable in the range of physiological pH conditions (e.g., pH 6.6–8.2).
source: Moreover, ABA-induced emission ratio changes of ABAleon1.1 were stable in the range of physiological pH conditions (e.g., pH 6.6–8.2; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly measured from pH titration experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: pRAB18-GFP expression was constitutive in guard cells when plants were grown at 70% relative humidity.
source: High ABA concentrations in guard cells were consistent with the constitutive guard cell expression of the ABA-induced reporter pRAB18-GFP when plants were grown at 70 % relative humidity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed from confocal images shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: pRAB18-GFP expression was further induced by ABA.
source: Expression of pRAB18-GFP was further induced by ABA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), however with stronger induction 2 days after transfer to 25 % relative humidity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,E).
evidence: This is directly observed from confocal images and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ABA uptake into guard cells and into the root occurred simultaneously in all three analyzed regions.
source: While ABA uptake into guard cells (Figure 3B) and into the root occurred simultaneously (Video 1) in all three analyzed regions (Figure 3H,K,N), a delay in the ABAleon2.1 response was observed in the hypocotyl (Figure 3E; Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed from time-resolved imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Video 1.

claim: A delay in the ABAleon2.1 response was observed in the hypocotyl.
source: While ABA uptake into guard cells (Figure 3B) and into the root occurred simultaneously (Video 1) in all three analyzed regions (Figure 3H,K,N), a delay in the ABAleon2.1 response was observed in the hypocotyl (Figure 3E; Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed from time-resolved imaging data shown in Figure 3 and Video 1.

claim: The data suggest a directional 'wave-like' ABA transport in the hypocotyl.
source: These data suggest a directional 'wave-like' ABA transport in the hypocotyl, which was also indicated in the ratio images (Figure 3F, Video 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-resolved imaging data showing sequential ABA uptake along the hypocotyl.

claim: Solvent control (EtOH) did not induce measurable emission ratio changes of ABAleon2.1.
source: These treatments did not induce measurable emission ratio changes of ABAleon2.1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: This is directly observed from control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The empty FRET-cassette showed no response to ABA.
source: In control seedlings expressing only the empty FRET-cassette no response to ABA was detected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is directly observed from control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: PYR1-ΔNABI1D413L incorporated in ABAleon2.1 are responsible for the ABA-induced emission ratio changes in Arabidopsis.
source: These data support, that PYR1-ΔNABI1D413L incorporated in ABAleon2.1 (Figure 1A) are responsible for the ABA-induced emission ratio changes in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of response in empty FRET cassette controls and the presence of response in ABAleon2.1.

claim: When ABA was applied to the root maturation zone, ABAleon2.1 emission ratios rapidly dropped, indicating ABA uptake into the root.
source: When ABA was applied to the root maturation zone (bottom chamber), ABAleon2.1 emission ratios rapidly dropped, indicating ABA uptake into the root (Figure 6D,J).
evidence: This is directly observed from experiments shown in Figure 6D,J.

claim: ABA was not transported upwards from root to hypocotyl within 180 min under the imposed conditions.
source: However, ABA was not transported upwards to the hypocotyl (top chamber) within 180 min under the imposed conditions (Figure 6D,I).
evidence: This is directly observed from experiments shown in Figure 6D,I.

claim: The data indicate a shoot to root ABA transport.
source: The above data indicate a shoot to root ABA transport (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is inferred from the long-distance transport experiments showing ABA movement from shoot to root.

claim: ABAleons were built on the strictly ABA-dependent interaction of PP2Cs with PYR1 and its phylogenetically close relatives.
source: ABAleons were built on the strictly ABA-dependent interaction of PP2Cs with PYR1 and its phylogenetically close relatives (Park et al., 2009; Santiago et al., 2009b; Nishimura et al., 2010), rather than the other members of the PYR/PYL/RCAR family, which have a higher probability of residing in a 'monomeric' state, and which can interact with PP2Cs even in the absence of ABA (Ma et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009; Dupeux et al., 2011; Hao et al., 2011).
evidence: This design choice is explained and supported by citations to published studies on ABA receptor properties.

claim: PYR1 and close homologs exhibit lower ABA affinities (Kd approximately 50–100 µM) than those of the 'monomeric' homologs (Kd approximately 1 µM).
source: PYR1 and close homologs exhibit lower ABA affinities (Kd ∼ 50–100 µM) than those of the 'monomeric' homologs (Kd ∼ 1 µM) (Ma et al., 2009; Miyazono et al., 2009; Santiago et al., 2009b; Dupeux et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on ABA receptor affinities.

claim: The ABA affinity of PYR/PYL/RCARs when bound to PP2Cs ranges between Kd approximately 20–125 nM.
source: In comparison, the ABA affinity of PYR/PYL/RCARs when bound to PP2Cs ranges between Kd ∼ 20–125 nM (Ma et al., 2009; Joshi-Saha et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ABAleons exhibit similar ABA affinities to endogenous PYR/PYL/RCARs or PYR/PYL/RCARs in complex with PP2Cs.
source: ABAleons exhibit similar ABA affinities to endogenous PYR/PYL/RCARs or PYR/PYL/RCARs in complex with PP2Cs (Figure 1E,F, Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Table 1), consistent with our findings, that ABAleon2.1 is able to detect changes in endogenous ABA concentrations (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by comparing measured ABAleon affinities with published values and by demonstrating detection of endogenous ABA changes.

claim: ABAleons exhibit higher affinity to the naturally occurring (+)-ABA than to (−)-ABA.
source: ABAleons exhibit higher affinity to the naturally occurring (+)-ABA than to (−)-ABA (Figure 7E,G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–G), and could potentially also bind to the synthetic ABA mimics pyrabactin and quinabactin (Park et al., 2009; Okamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly measured from in vitro characterization experiments comparing (+)- and (−)-ABA binding.

claim: ABAleons could potentially also bind to the synthetic ABA mimics pyrabactin and quinabactin.
source: ABAleons exhibit higher affinity to the naturally occurring (+)-ABA than to (−)-ABA (Figure 7E,G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–G), and could potentially also bind to the synthetic ABA mimics pyrabactin and quinabactin (Park et al., 2009; Okamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculated based on the known binding properties of PYR1 to these compounds as reported in cited studies.

claim: The homologous H139 in PYL3 was important for ABA stereospecificity.
source: These results are consistent with recent findings that the homologous H139 in PYL3 was important for ABA stereospecificity (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: ABAleon2.11, carrying the PYR1H60P mutation, exhibited spectral characteristics comparable to ABA-bound ABAleon2.1.
source: ABAleon2.11, carrying the PYR1H60P mutation (Dupeux et al., 2011), exhibited spectral characteristics comparable to ABA-bound ABAleon2.1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is directly measured from in vitro characterization experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The PYR1H60P protein may form an alternative interaction interface with PP2Cs, even in the absence of ABA.
source: This is consistent with the notion, that the PYR1H60P protein may form an alternative interaction interface with PP2Cs, even in the absence of ABA (Dupeux et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the spectral characteristics of ABAleon2.11 and is consistent with published structural studies.

claim: Over-expression of the ABA receptors PYR1, PYL2 and PYL5 induces ABA hypersensitivity in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis, over-expression of the ABA receptors PYR1, PYL2 and PYL5 induces ABA hypersensitivity (Figure 5; Santiago et al., 2009b; Mosquna et al., 2011), while ectopic expression of the PP2Cs ABI1 and HAB1 decreases ABA sensitivity (Figure 5; Santiago et al., 2009b; Nishimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 and citations to published studies.

claim: Ectopic expression of the PP2Cs ABI1 and HAB1 decreases ABA sensitivity in Arabidopsis.
source: In Arabidopsis, over-expression of the ABA receptors PYR1, PYL2 and PYL5 induces ABA hypersensitivity (Figure 5; Santiago et al., 2009b; Mosquna et al., 2011), while ectopic expression of the PP2Cs ABI1 and HAB1 decreases ABA sensitivity (Figure 5; Santiago et al., 2009b; Nishimura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 and citations to published studies.

claim: ABAleon2.1 might sequester a certain amount of physiologically relevant ABA in certain tissues and cell types due to its high affinity, thus causing ABA hyposensitivity.
source: Because ABAleon2.1 did not exhibit any phosphatase activity in vitro (Figure 1H), it can be speculated, that ABAleon2.1 might sequester a certain amount of physiologically relevant ABA in certain tissues and cell types due to its high affinity (Figure 1E,F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D; Table 1), thus causing ABA hyposensitivity (Figure 5).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed ABA hyposensitivity and the high affinity of ABAleon2.1 for ABA.

claim: Mutants defective in ABA signaling may compensate by up-regulating ABA levels.
source: Mutants defective in ABA signaling may compensate by up-regulating ABA levels, as reported previously (Nakashima et al., 2009) and could also up-regulate ABA transport activity (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed accelerated ABA uptake in the pyl4ple mutant and is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Knock out of ABA receptors may affect ABA buffering capacity.
source: Alternatively, knock out of ABA receptors may also affect ABA buffering capacity (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is speculated as an alternative explanation for the accelerated ABA uptake in the pyl4ple mutant.

claim: ABA induces cytoplasmic alkalinization of guard cells.
source: ABA induces cytoplasmic alkalinization of guard cells (Blatt and Armstrong, 1993; Islam et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: In guard cells of Vicia faba, cytoplasmic pH was found to be 7.67 and increased 0.27 units upon ABA treatment.
source: In guard cells of Vicia faba, cytoplasmic pH was found to be 7.67 and increased 0.27 units upon ABA treatment (Blatt and Armstrong, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Cytoplasmic pH in roots was 7.3 and could increase to 7.7.
source: Cytoplasmic pH in roots was 7.3 and could increase to 7.7 (Bibikova et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Overall ABA levels range from 30–50 ng/g dry-weight in non-stressed plants.
source: Overall ABA levels range from 30–50 ng/g dry-weight in non-stressed plants (Forcat et al., 2008; Geng et al., 2013), which can increase up to 30-fold in response to limited water conditions (Harris et al., 1988; Harris and Outlaw 1991; Christmann et al., 2007; Ikegami et al., 2009; Geng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies measuring ABA levels.

claim: ABA levels can increase up to 30-fold in response to limited water conditions.
source: Overall ABA levels range from 30–50 ng/g dry-weight in non-stressed plants (Forcat et al., 2008; Geng et al., 2013), which can increase up to 30-fold in response to limited water conditions (Harris et al., 1988; Harris and Outlaw 1991; Christmann et al., 2007; Ikegami et al., 2009; Geng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies measuring ABA levels under stress.

claim: In Vicia faba guard cells ABA concentrations were approximately 0.7 fg/cell pair in unstressed and approximately 17.7 fg/cell pair in stressed guard cells.
source: In Vicia faba guard cells ABA concentrations were ∼ 0.7 fg/cell pair in unstressed and ∼ 17.7 fg/cell pair in stressed guard cells (Harris et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: ABA concentrations in stressed guard cells were estimated to be in the range of approximately 15 µM.
source: ABA concentrations in stressed guard cells were estimated to be in the range of ∼ 15 µM (Harris et al., 1988; Harris and Outlaw 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Unstressed guard cell ABA concentration would be approximately 500 nM based on extrapolation.
source: Extrapolating from these values, unstressed guard cell ABA concentration would be ∼ 500 nM.
evidence: This is calculated by extrapolating from published measurements of ABA in stressed guard cells.

claim: Such approximations would be consistent with the partial saturation and reduced response of ABAleon2.1 in guard cells.
source: Such approximations would be consistent with the partial saturation and reduced response of ABAleon2.1 in guard cells (Figure 3A–C) and with strong expression of the ABA-induced reporter pRAB18-GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing estimated ABA concentrations with ABAleon2.1 responses and pRAB18-GFP expression.

claim: Jones et al. developed ABACUS-type ABA reporters with biochemical properties complementary to ABAleons.
source: During the course of our ABAleon research we found, that Jones et al. developed ABACUS-type ABA reporters, however with biochemical properties complementary to ABAleons (Jones et al., 2014).
evidence: This acknowledges concurrent work by another group and is supported by a citation.

claim: ABAleons and ABACUS could be utilized to study novel aspects of ABA signaling in intact plants.
source: Thus, ABAleons and ABACUS could be utilized to study novel aspects of ABA signaling in intact plants.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about potential applications based on the complementary properties of the two reporter systems.
